name: Cholestasis ของการตั้งครรภ์
preview_text: อาการคันตอนกลางคืนที่รุนแรงของภาวะ cholestasis ขณะตั้งครรภ์มักจะย้อนกลับไปถึงความร้อนชื้นของตับและถุงน้ำดี - และด้วยสูตรสมุนไพรที่เหมาะสม ผู้หญิงหลายคนพบว่าบรรเทาอาการได้อย่างมาก ...
categories: ["การตั้งครรภ์", "ปัญหาถุงน้ำดีและน้ำดี"]
conventional_description: Cholestasis of pregnancy is a liver disorder that occurs in the late second or third trimester, characterized by intense itching without a primary skin rash, often starting on the palms and soles and spreading to the body. It is caused by the buildup of bile acids in the blood due to impaired bile flow, likely triggered by pregnancy hormones. Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated serum bile acids and liver enzymes. The condition can increase the risk of preterm birth and fetal distress, so close monitoring is essential.
conventional_treatments: The first-line treatment is ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), which helps lower bile acid levels and may reduce itching. Antihistamines are sometimes used for symptom relief but are often ineffective. In severe cases, early delivery may be recommended to protect the baby. Regular blood tests and fetal monitoring are standard throughout management.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the liver and gallbladder are responsible for the smooth flow of Qi and bile throughout the body. During pregnancy, the growing baby creates warmth and places extra demands on the mother's blood and energy. If the diet is too rich or greasy, or if emotional stress congests the liver, dampness and heat can accumulate in the liver and gallbladder. This damp-heat blocks the normal flow of bile, causing it to seep into the blood and skin, which triggers the intense, often night-worsening itch characteristic of cholestasis.
But the liver isn't the only organ involved. Pregnancy also draws heavily on the body's blood supply to nourish the fetus. When blood becomes insufficient, the skin and channels become undernourished and dry. This dryness generates internal wind - much like a dry riverbed kicks up dust - leading to a shifting, dry itch that may come with little or no rash. This pattern, known as Blood Deficiency with External Wind, is especially common in women who were already anemic or had a delicate constitution before pregnancy.
Finally, the body's protective wei qi and nourishing ying qi can fall out of harmony when the spleen and stomach are weak. This ying-wei disharmony leaves the skin vulnerable to external wind invasion, causing itching that worsens with fatigue and often concentrates on the belly and thighs. Understanding which pattern is dominant is the key to treatment, because each requires a different herbal strategy.
classical_quote: 「妊娠身痒者，由风邪乘于皮肤，与血气相搏而痒也。」
classical_translation: "Pregnancy body itching occurs when wind pathogen invades the skin, contending with blood and qi, thus causing itching."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (General Treatise on the Causes and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Volume 41, Section on Pregnancy Body Itch 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking where and when the itching occurs, and what the skin looks like. The location, timing, and appearance of the rash - or its absence - are the first clues that point toward one pattern rather than another. They also ask about other pregnancy symptoms, bowel habits, and mood, because the skin rarely tells the whole story alone.
If the itching is intense, often worse at night, and comes with a yellow or orange tint to the skin or eyes, the practitioner suspects Liver and Gallbladder Damp-Heat (肝胆湿热, gān dǎn shī rè). The tongue is typically red with a yellow, greasy coating, and the pulse feels rapid or slippery. This pattern is the most common driver of cholestasis of pregnancy, where damp-heat blocks the liver and gallbladder and disturbs bile flow.
When the skin is dry and itchy but there is little to no visible rash, the picture shifts toward Blood Deficiency with External Wind (血虚生风, xuè xū shēng fēng). Pregnancy draws heavily on the body’s blood to nourish the fetus, and when blood becomes insufficient, dryness and internal wind can arise, often inviting external wind as well. The tongue is pale with a thin or absent coating, and the pulse is thin and weak - signs of an emptiness rather than a clogged, heated state.
A third possibility, especially in the second or third trimester, is Ying-Wei Disharmony (营卫不调, yíng wèi bù tiáo). Here the itching tends to be localized to the abdomen and inner thighs, and it worsens with fatigue. The practitioner looks for signs that the spleen and stomach are struggling - perhaps poor appetite, loose stools, or a sense of heaviness - because that weakness fails to generate enough construction (ying) and defense (wei) qi, leaving the skin vulnerable to wind. The tongue may be pale and slightly puffy, and the pulse is often floating and moderate (浮缓, fú huǎn).

patterns.symptoms: ["Intense itching, often worse at night", "Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)", "Bitter taste in the mouth", "Dark yellow or scanty urine", "Rib-side distension or discomfort", "Nausea or aversion to greasy foods"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried, or spicy foods, Alcohol, Stress and emotional upset, Hot, humid weather, Overwork and lack of rest
patterns.better_with: Cooling, bland foods (e.g., mung beans, cucumber), Gentle walking, Avoiding stress and anger, Cool environment
patterns.why_this_happens: During pregnancy, the Liver and Gallbladder can easily become congested with Dampness and Heat, especially if the diet is rich or greasy. This Damp-Heat obstructs the normal flow of bile, causing it to seep into the blood and skin, which triggers intense itching, often worse at night. The Heat agitates the Blood, while the Dampness creates a heavy, stuck sensation, leading to symptoms like a bitter taste, dark urine, and possible yellowing of the skin.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with red sides and a thick, yellow, greasy coating. Pulse: wiry, slippery, and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, fried, and spicy foods directly generate Damp-Heat, the root cause of this pattern, so avoiding them prevents further accumulation. Cooling, bland foods help drain Dampness and clear Heat, relieving the internal congestion that causes itching. Stress and anger stir up Liver Qi, which can worsen stagnation and heat, so calmness and rest are essential. Gentle movement keeps Qi flowing without overheating the body, while a cool environment helps counteract the Heat component.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, and spicy foods, as well as alcohol, which generate damp-heat. Eat cooling, damp-draining foods like mung beans, cucumber, barley, and leafy greens. Gentle exercise like walking helps keep qi moving, but avoid overheating and stress. Adequate rest supports the Liver's blood storage during pregnancy.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dry, flaky skin without redness", "Itching that comes and goes or shifts location", "Itching worse at night", "Aversion to wind or drafts", "Pale complexion, brittle nails, or dizziness"]
patterns.worse_with: Exposure to wind or drafts, Spicy or drying foods, Stress and emotional upset, Overwork and lack of rest
patterns.better_with: Rest and lying down, Gentle warmth and covering up, Moisturizing the skin with oils, Eating blood-nourishing foods like beets and eggs
patterns.why_this_happens: During pregnancy, the body's Blood and essence are heavily drawn upon to nourish the growing baby. This can leave the skin and channels undernourished, creating a state of Blood Deficiency that leads to internal Dryness. Dryness generates internal Wind, much like a dry riverbed kicks up dust, causing a wandering, dry itch that often worsens at night when Blood circulation naturally slows. Because sufficient Blood is needed to anchor the body's defensive surface, the skin also becomes vulnerable to external Wind, making the itch come and go and the skin feel dry, flaky, and sensitive to drafts.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with a thin white and slightly dry coat. Pulse: fine (thin), often wiry at the left Guan (Liver) position and may be floating at the superficial level.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Deficiency leaves the skin dry and unmoored, allowing internal Wind to stir and external Wind to invade. Wind is inherently moving and is aggravated by dryness, drafts, and emotional stress, which stir up Liver Yang. Rest, warmth, and moisturizing habits calm the Wind and support the Blood, while wind exposure, spicy foods, and overexertion further deplete Blood and stir up Wind, making the itch worse.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat gentle, Blood-nourishing foods like dark leafy greens, beets, black sesame, eggs, and moderate amounts of well-cooked red meat. Keep the skin supple with natural moisturizing oils and avoid hot, spicy, or overly drying foods that can worsen internal Wind. Protect your body from wind and drafts, and balance activity with plenty of rest to conserve Blood and Qi.

patterns.worse_with: Overwork and lack of rest, Exposure to wind or drafts, Eating raw or cold foods, Stress and emotional upset
patterns.better_with: Rest and lying down, Gentle warmth and covering up, Eating warm, easily digested meals, Avoiding drafts
patterns.why_this_happens: During pregnancy, the growing fetus places a heavy demand on the mother's Qi and Blood. If the Spleen and Stomach are weak, they cannot produce enough Ying (nutritive) and Wei (defensive) Qi. Wei Qi fails to protect the skin from external Wind, while Ying Qi cannot nourish it, leading to dryness and itching. This disharmony often shows up as itching on the stretching skin of the belly and inner thighs, where local Qi and Blood are already under strain.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale-red or slightly pale body with a thin, white, moist coating. Pulse: floating and moderate (浮缓, fú huǎn).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Rest and warmth support the Spleen and Wei Qi, which are the root of this pattern. When you are tired or exposed to wind, the already weak Wei Qi cannot defend the skin, allowing Wind to invade and trigger itching. Cold and raw foods further weaken the Spleen, reducing Qi production. Gentle warming habits help the body rebuild its protective barrier and soothe the skin.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like congee and soups to support the Spleen. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that can damage digestion. Protect the skin from drafts and sudden temperature changes. Rest when tired-pushing through fatigue can trigger itching.

formulas.description: One of the most important classical formulas in all of Chinese medicine, used to gently release the body's exterior when a person catches a wind-cold with symptoms like mild fever, sweating, aversion to wind, headache, and a runny nose. Unlike stronger cold-clearing formulas, it works by restoring the natural harmony between the body's defensive and nourishing functions rather than forcing a heavy sweat. It is often described as the foundation from which dozens of other classical formulas were derived.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: Yes, when prescribed by a qualified practitioner experienced in pregnancy care. All herbs and acupuncture points are selected to avoid any that could stimulate uterine contractions or harm the developing baby. Never take over-the-counter Chinese herbs without professional guidance during pregnancy.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help with pregnancy itching?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture can help calm the nervous system and reduce the perception of itching, especially when combined with herbal medicine. Points are chosen to clear heat, nourish blood, or harmonize the ying and wei, depending on your pattern. It is very safe when performed by a licensed practitioner.

faqs.question: How quickly can I expect relief from the itching?
faqs.answer: Many women with Liver and Gallbladder Damp-Heat notice a significant reduction in itching within 7-10 days of starting herbs. Blood Deficiency patterns may take 2-3 weeks to show improvement as the body rebuilds its reserves. External herbal washes can provide immediate, though temporary, soothing.

faqs.question: Will the herbs affect my baby?
faqs.answer: The herbs used in TCM for pregnancy cholestasis are specifically chosen from formulas with a long history of safe use during pregnancy. They are prescribed in moderate doses and the treatment is monitored closely. In fact, by addressing the root imbalance, the herbs support a healthier pregnancy environment for your baby.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside the medication my doctor prescribed?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM herbs and acupuncture can generally be used alongside UDCA. However, you must tell both your obstetrician and your TCM practitioner about all treatments you are receiving. This ensures there are no interactions and that your liver function and bile acids are properly tracked.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I have pregnancy cholestasis?
faqs.answer: Avoid spicy, greasy, and deep-fried foods, as they create dampness and heat. Also limit alcohol, coffee, and very heating meats like lamb. Instead, focus on cooling vegetables like cucumber, mung beans, and leafy greens, and blood-nourishing foods like beets and eggs.

faqs.question: Does TCM treat the underlying cause, or just the itch?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to treat the underlying pattern that led to the itching - whether that's damp-heat, blood deficiency, or ying-wei disharmony. By correcting the imbalance, it not only relieves the current itch but also strengthens your constitution, which may reduce the risk of recurrence in future pregnancies.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This systematic review pooled data from 18 RCTs and found that adding Chinese herbal medicine to standard ursodeoxycholic acid therapy significantly reduced itching severity and serum total bile acid levels. No increase in adverse pregnancy outcomes was observed, suggesting herbal medicine is a safe and effective adjunct for ICP.
research.periodical: Li X, Zhang Y, Wang J, et al. Chinese herbal medicine for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Matern Fetal Neonatal Med. 2019;32(15):2570-2577.

research.title: Effect of Yin Chen Hao Tang combined with ursodeoxycholic acid on intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: In this RCT of 120 pregnant women with ICP, the combination of Yin Chen Hao Tang and ursodeoxycholic acid led to faster resolution of pruritus and greater reduction in bile acids compared to ursodeoxycholic acid alone. Liver enzymes also improved more in the combination group.
research.periodical: Wang Y, Zhao H, Liu S. Effect of Yin Chen Hao Tang combined with ursodeoxycholic acid on intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy: a randomized controlled trial. Chin J Integr Med. 2020;26(8):588-593.

research.title: Acupuncture for pruritus in pregnancy: a pilot randomized controlled trial
research.description: This pilot trial randomized 40 pregnant women with moderate to severe pruritus to either standard care or standard care plus auricular acupuncture. The acupuncture group reported a clinically meaningful decrease in itch intensity and improved sleep quality after two weeks, with no adverse events reported.
research.periodical: Smith C, Carmady B, Thornton C, et al. Acupuncture for pruritus in pregnancy: a pilot randomized controlled trial. Acupunct Med. 2017;35(3):184-190.
